submissive

/suhb-MIS-iv/ · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Submissive means readily yielding to another's authority or will — letting your own judgment give way and obeying without resistance.

The once-blunt negotiator turned oddly submissive whenever the chairman entered, conceding terms she had rejected an hour earlier.

Example

Everyone at the pass could see the head chef had misread the ticket — table nine had ordered the salmon. The new line cook opened his mouth, caught the chef's glare, and closed it again. He plated the wrong dish exactly as directed, apologized for a delay that was not his fault, and asked, quietly, whether the chef would like the garnish changed too. Three months in, the kitchen had taught him to be submissive: whatever he knew, authority outranked it.

The cook has judgment of his own — he knows the ticket was misread — but he lets it collapse the moment authority pushes back, obeying without resistance. That surrender of one's own will to another's is exactly what submissive describes.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

compliant: Compliant means going along with rules, requests, and procedures — you comply with a policy, a deadline, a doctor's orders. Submissive is about persons, not paperwork: it describes a will bowing to someone's authority, often against the yielder's own judgment, even when nothing has actually been asked.

docile: Docile means naturally mild and easily led — a docile temperament simply has no fight in it to begin with. Submissive describes the yielding itself, in the moment: a strong-willed person with plenty of fight can still turn submissive when authority stares them down.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

defiant: openly resisting authority

assertive: stating your own position with confidence

Where it sits · how completely one's own will gives way

deferential → submissive → servile

deferential vs. submissive: Deferential is milder than submissive: a deferential junior yields politely out of respect while keeping a will of her own, but a submissive one lets that will give way altogether.

servile vs. submissive: Servile goes further than submissive: submission surrenders your judgment when authority presses, while servility adds eager, fawning self-abasement — the flattery volunteered before anyone even asks.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — sub-: under, beneath

Root — miss: to send; to let go (Latin mittere, missus)

Suffix — -ive: adjective-forming: inclined to, given to

Put it together: Sub- (under) plus miss (to send) built Latin submittere, 'to place under' — to submit is literally to send yourself under someone else's authority. This unit's adjective-forming -ive suffix then turns the act into a standing tendency: a submissive person is one inclined to go under, whose will lowers itself whenever authority leans in. The sending root is one of Latin's busiest — dismiss, transmit, emit, and permission all ride on it.

Use the root in a new word: remiss: Reviewers later called the committee remiss for approving the bridge design after a single afternoon's discussion.

Root Check

Word Choice

disapproving to neutral; usually implies a will that ought to push back

Submissive takes 'to' ('submissive to the board') and almost always carries a raised eyebrow: it suggests the yielding goes further than it should. Keep it apart from cooperative, which shares work rather than surrendering will, and from this unit's impassive, which hides feeling behind a still face — an impassive negotiator may be yielding nothing at all. And do not confuse the adjective with the verb's paperwork sense: an essay is submitted, never submissive.
